mstts:express-as.prosody: Welcome to a journey that winds through the very heart of America—where every backroad, every diner, and every small town holds a story waiting to be discovered. You ever wondered what lies beyond the highways we speed down, or the towns we just pass by on our way to somewhere else? Together, we’ll step into the world Bill Bryson paints in The Lost Continent: Travels in Small-Town America. With Bryson’s signature wit and warmth, we’ll wander streets full of nostalgia, discover the quirks and charms of places that feel both familiar and unexpected, and find ourselves laughing one minute and feeling a quiet ache the next. What makes a place feel like home? How do memories of childhood mix with the realities of today? As we explore these questions, we’ll meet unforgettable locals, stumble across faded landmarks, and soak in the enduring spirit of communities shaped by both history and change. So, let’s set out together and discover the mosaic of America—its contradictions, its comforts, and the longing for belonging that ties us all together. Who knows? In these overlooked corners, we just might find something we’ve been searching for all along.

Chapter 1. Searching for the America That Once Was
You ever notice that little ache when you look back at your childhood? It’s almost like missing a place that’s quietly slipped away. For a lot of us, small-town America isn’t just a memory—it’s almost a legend now. We think of quiet streets, neighbors who wave from their porches, and that deep feeling of belonging.
So, where does the journey begin? With longing, of course. A hope that maybe, just maybe, those places still exist somewhere beyond the main highways.
Picture this: a modest home, a son, and a father who loved nothing more than a good road trip. Those family drives, humming along backroads with a sense of adventure in the air, left a mark that never quite faded. The father—he was the kind of guy who thought the real heart of America lived in its small towns, not in any big city. He’d plan trips that skipped the interstates, sticking to the roads where folks still waved and diners served up pie that tasted like it came from someone’s grandma.
Years later, that son finds himself with a full tank, a pile of maps, and that same restless curiosity. This time, it’s his turn. He’s out to retrace some of those old routes—and maybe blaze a few new ones. But it’s not just about the scenery. It’s about finding out if the America he remembers is still hiding out there, somewhere between the endless stretches of highway. There’s excitement, sure, but also a little skepticism. After all, time changes everything, and nostalgia? Well, it tends to blur the rough edges, doesn’t it?
The first towns along the way are a mix of old and new, familiar and strange. Some feel frozen in time—with faded storefronts and quiet main streets. Others? They’ve been swallowed up by the same chain stores you see everywhere, their unique charm replaced by something a little too familiar. Pretty soon, it’s clear: searching for the “lost continent” of small-town America is really about facing change. And sometimes, it’s about finding comfort in the past—even when things look different.
There’s plenty of humor and a few headaches along the way. Maybe you stop at a roadside spot claiming the “World’s Largest Ball of Twine,” and all you find is a dusty display and a bored teenager at the ticket booth. Or you end up in a motel room that smells a little musty, where the TV barely works. But somehow, even these little hiccups have their own charm. It’s a reminder that life doesn’t have to be polished or perfect to be special.
Chatting with locals, you hear a mix of pride and a little resignation. Some folks talk about the good old days, while others seem ready to move on. The world’s gotten bigger and faster, and these towns have been left a bit behind. But you know what? There’s also a quiet resilience—a stubborn belief that small-town life still matters, even if it’s changed.
And as the miles roll by, something shifts. The traveler starts to realize this journey isn’t just about finding lost places. It’s about understanding himself—how childhood memories, family stories, and today’s reality all tangle together. The search for that lost America? It becomes a way to make sense of change, of loss, and most of all, of hope. Because somewhere out there, some of the best parts of the past just might still be waiting.

Chapter 2: The Reality Behind the Myth of Small-Town America
Picture this: you set out on the open road, head buzzing with old stories and your heart full of hope. Maybe you’re chasing that classic postcard vision—neat little streets, friendly faces, and a tight-knit community that feels like it’s always been there. But as you roll through the miles, you start to notice something. The real small-town America? It’s a whole lot more layered than those picture-perfect myths.
Imagine driving through the Midwest. Cornfields stretch on forever, silos dot the horizon, and every so often, a small town appears—complete with a water tower and a main street lined by buildings that have seen better days. Some towns really do feel welcoming: lawns are trimmed, people are gathered outside the hardware store, swapping stories. But then, you pass others where the paint’s peeling from empty storefronts, and the only movement is a dog lazily napping in the shade.
Stop for lunch at a local diner, and you’ll hear snippets of daily life drifting across the booths—talk of weather, crops, and who won last night’s high school game. The waitress, with her practiced smile, keeps the coffee flowing and calls everyone “hon.” There’s something comforting about the routine, isn’t there? It’s easy to see why folks look back on these places with such fondness—a sense of belonging that’s tough to find in a busy city.
But if you look a little closer, you’ll sense something else—a quiet undercurrent of loss. Many of these towns are shrinking. Young people, searching for bigger dreams, have moved on. The factories that once kept families afloat have closed their doors. You might meet someone running the only gas station left in town, reminiscing about the days when the highway brought crowds, not just cars speeding by without a second glance.
And sometimes, you stumble into moments that are just, well, a bit absurd. In one small town, you might find a museum dedicated entirely to antique toasters. The guide, a retired teacher, gives the tour with genuine excitement, turning an odd little collection into something memorable. It’s both charming and a little bittersweet—a reminder that, sometimes, people hang on to the smallest things when everything else feels like it’s slipping away.
As you keep traveling, you start to notice how chain stores and fast-food signs are edging out the unique quirks that once set each town apart. That familiar neon glow? It’s everywhere now. It’s a subtle kind of erasure, one that sneaks up on you until suddenly, it feels like what made these places special is fading into the background.
But even with all that, you’ll still find moments of real connection. Maybe a family invites you to their picnic in the park, sharing stories and passing around homemade potato salad. Or maybe an older couple sits on a bench, remembering when the town square was the heart of it all. In these moments, you get a glimpse of the community spirit that once defined small-town life.
By the end of this part of the journey, one thing’s clear: the myth of small-town America is both true and not. The warmth and simplicity are definitely there—but so are the challenges, and the disappointments. Nostalgia can be a comfort, sure, but it can also keep us from seeing what’s really happening right now. So, the search for that lost continent? It’s not just about finding what’s disappeared—it’s about understanding what’s still here, quietly holding on.

Chapter 3: Regional Differences and the Patchwork of American Identity.
Imagine driving across America, watching the scenery—and even the people—change right outside your window. Every state, every town, has its own flavor. The way folks talk, the food they serve, the very air you breathe—it all shifts as you move from one region to the next.
Down South, you can almost feel the history in the heavy, humid air. The sound of cicadas fills the evenings, and towns gather around old courthouses shaded by sprawling oaks. Life moves a little slower here. Conversations stretch out over glasses of sweet tea, and stories from the past—some celebrated, some whispered—still shape daily life. In one small town, the Civil War isn’t just a history lesson; it’s woven into the present, always close to the surface.
Then, as you roll into the Midwest, everything feels a bit different. The land opens up—fields everywhere, sky stretching endlessly above. Here, towns are built for practicality, not show. People are welcoming, but a bit reserved. They’ll lend a hand in a heartbeat, but you might have to earn their trust before they share much about themselves. Picture a classic county fair, with a pie-eating contest and a tractor pull front and center. Tradition means a lot, and change? Well, it tends to take its time.
Up in the Northeast, the towns are older, filled with brick buildings and narrow streets that practically echo with history. But there’s a restless energy too—people always seem to be on the move. One morning, you find yourself in a tiny coastal town, watching fishermen bring in their catch as the first light touches the water. The air is salty and full of promise, hinting at both old stories and new possibilities.
And then there’s the West. Out here, the landscape is bold—mountains, deserts, that endless sky. Towns feel scattered, sometimes barely clinging to the edge of civilization. There’s a wild sense of freedom, but also a certain loneliness. You meet a woman running a tiny bookstore in a town of fewer than a thousand people. She talks about how tough it can be, living so far from everything, but also about the peace she’s found out here.
No matter where you go, you notice something: people hold tight to their identities. Maybe it’s a barbecue recipe that’s been in the family forever, or a festival the whole town looks forward to every year. There’s a real pride in these traditions. But there’s tension too—a worry that all this local flavor is at risk, slowly fading as the world outside pushes in and things start to look the same everywhere.
It’s easy to miss these differences if you’re just passing through. Most folks only catch the surface, never seeing how deeply culture and history shape a place. But if you look closer, you realize America isn’t just one thing—it’s a patchwork, a mix of identities, each with its own story and struggles.
By the end of this part of the journey, you feel both more connected to the country and more aware of just how complex it really is. That search for the “lost continent”? Maybe it’s not about finding one single America, but about learning to appreciate all the diversity that makes this country what it is.

Chapter 4: The Absurdities and Oddities of the American Road.
Traveling across America by car is a wild mix of wonder and frustration. The open road feels like an invitation to freedom, but let’s be honest—it’s also a highway full of quirks, weird little inconveniences, and moments that make you shake your head in disbelief. If you’ve ever spent any time roaming the highways or winding through backroads, you know exactly what I mean. Those oddball moments? They end up becoming part of your story—a reminder that sometimes, the journey really is more interesting than wherever you’re headed.
Pretty quickly, you realize not all roads are the same. Some just stretch on forever, straight as an arrow, bordered by endless fields and—every so often—a billboard promising the world’s biggest ball of twine or something equally random. Then there are those roads that twist their way through mountains or forests, giving you jaw-dropping views and just a little bit of worry that you might end up completely lost. Road signs? They can be downright confusing, and even the best maps don’t always match up with what you see out your window. But that’s part of the adventure, isn’t it? You start to develop a knack for handling these curveballs, and you learn to laugh when you inevitably take a wrong turn.
And let’s talk about motels. They become your second home on the road, and each one has its own... personality. Some are sparkling clean, with owners who greet you like an old friend and take real pride in the place. Others? Well, let’s just say you might encounter flickering lights and mysterious stains that make you rethink your life choices. You start to appreciate the little victories—a working air conditioner, a hot shower, a mattress that doesn’t swallow you whole. There’s even this quiet sense of camaraderie with other travelers. Everyone’s just trying to get some rest before the next leg of the journey, and there’s a kind of unspoken understanding in that.
Then there are the roadside attractions—a world all their own. Imagine giant fiberglass animals towering over the highway, or museums dedicated to topics so obscure you can’t help but be curious. There’s that “mystery spot” where gravity seems to break all the rules, or a gift shop filled with souvenirs nobody really needs but everyone secretly wants. You can’t help but wonder—why do people build these things, and why do we feel compelled to pull over and see them for ourselves? It’s equal parts amusement and pure bewilderment.
Food on the road is its own adventure too. Diners and fast-food joints pop up everywhere, all promising a taste of home. You’ll sample everything from greasy burgers to homemade pies, and you never really know what you’re gonna get. Sometimes, the food’s nothing special. But then, there are those moments when a simple meal in a tiny town turns into the highlight of your day—a reminder that genuine hospitality can still surprise you.
Of course, the road isn’t always excitement and discovery. There are those long, lonely stretches where the scenery never seems to change, and the miles just drag on. That’s when the radio becomes your best friend—music, news, the comfort of other voices keeping you company. Sometimes, it’s just you and the steady rhythm of the tires on the pavement for miles on end.
But here’s where it gets interesting. It’s in those weird, inconvenient, or downright absurd moments that you find the real meaning of the trip. Those challenges and little frustrations—they become the stories you tell later, the memories that stick with you long after you’ve unpacked. The oddities aren’t just obstacles. They’re woven into the fabric of the journey, reminding you that travel isn’t just about new places—it’s about learning to expect the unexpected, and finding the humor in everyday life.
By the time you reach the end of this road, you start to genuinely appreciate all those quirks that make the American highway so unique. The search for the “lost continent” isn’t really about finding the perfect small town or the ideal experience. It’s about embracing the messiness, the unpredictability, and the surprises that come with real life. And as the journey rolls on, it’s these oddities and surprises that make every single day on the road one of a kind.

Chapter 5: Personal Reflections and the Power of Nostalgia
As the journey continues and the scenery changes from one region to the next, something shifts inside. This search for small-town America starts to feel a lot less about the places themselves—and a lot more about the memories and emotions they stir up.
Nostalgia really steps in here. It’s warm, even comforting, but there’s also an ache to it. Sometimes, it can be both a gentle guide and a real challenge.
It’s impossible not to think about family along the way—especially parents. For our traveler, his father’s love of the open road is the real spark behind this whole adventure. Suddenly, childhood memories come rushing back: those long car rides with everyone packed in, the thrill of stopping at a roadside motel, the simple joy of a picnic on the grass. It’s all so vivid—and yet, there’s a bittersweet edge, knowing the world has changed and some of those moments just can’t be relived.
In one small town, he wanders into a park that looks just like the one from his own childhood. Kids are laughing on the swings, parents are chatting on benches, and for a second, it feels like he’s stepped right back in time.
But then he glances over and spots a strip mall, with its row of familiar chain stores, and the present comes rushing back in.
It’s funny how the past and present can sit side by side like that—each one changing the way we remember the other.
Talking with locals, the conversation almost always drifts to change. The older folks talk with a mix of pride and regret about how things used to be. You can hear it in their voices: the memories, the longing, the pride in what their town once was. Younger people, though, have their eyes on the future. They’re dreaming about bigger cities and new adventures.
And somewhere in the middle, our traveler realizes how powerful nostalgia really is. It can inspire, but it can also hold you back—sometimes making it tough to appreciate what’s right in front of you.
There are plenty of quiet moments, too. At the end of a long day, sitting in a motel room, he thinks back on the places he’s seen and the people he’s met. Some towns match the memories—others, not so much. But each stop has given him something: a story, a lesson, a reminder that this search for meaning never really ends.
The deeper the journey goes, the clearer it gets—our own history shapes the way we see everything. The places that matter most are the ones tied to personal memories or feelings.
It dawns on him that this “lost continent” he’s been chasing isn’t just a spot on the map. It’s a state of mind, a way of seeing the world that values simplicity, connection, and the feeling of truly belonging.
By this point, he’s come to accept something important: the past can’t be fully recovered. But that doesn’t mean it’s gone. Those memories, those stories, and those feelings—they’re all still here, woven right into the present.
So, this search for small-town America becomes more than nostalgia. It turns into a way to honor the past, while learning to embrace the reality of change.
The road stretches on, with new towns to explore and fresh stories waiting around every bend. The journey isn’t over—not by a long shot. But the lessons learned bring a sense of comfort... and hope.
Maybe the lost continent will never be found in full. But its spirit? It lives on—in the hearts of those who remember, and in those quiet corners of the country, where the past and present gently meet.

Chapter 6: The Heartland’s Quiet Resilience. Picture this: dusk settling over the heartland, fields stretching as far as you can see, the last bit of sunlight glinting off old grain silos. Off in the distance, there’s the low, steady hum of a tractor finishing up its work for the day. Now, imagine a traveler arriving in a town that feels almost untouched by time. The main street’s nearly empty, and the only place open is a little grocery store run by a couple who’ve lived there their whole lives. Step inside, and you’re greeted by the cozy scent of coffee and old wood. The store owners welcome you with a gentle, cautious warmth. They’re curious—what brings someone new to this quiet corner? Before long, over steaming cups of coffee, the stories begin to flow. They talk about the floods that nearly washed the town away, and how neighbors rallied to rebuild. About kids who left for bigger cities, and parents who chose to stay behind. There’s definitely a sense of loss, but it’s mixed with an undeniable pride. The couple shares how important it is to keep showing up for each other, especially when things get tough. Later, as the traveler wanders through the quiet streets, he notices the faded signs and boarded-up windows. Sure, it’d be easy to focus on what’s been lost. But then he spots small sparks of hope—a new mural painted by local kids, a community garden where folks gather on weekends. That’s when it hits him: resilience doesn’t always grab your attention. Sometimes, it’s the quiet choice to keep going, to care for a place even when it feels like the world’s moved on. In another town, a retired teacher has started a book club that meets in the old library. It’s a small group, but the conversations are anything but dull. They chat about everything—from local history to the latest bestseller—finding connection in the simple act of reading together. The traveler’s invited to join, and for one evening, he’s part of their circle. It’s proof that community can spring up in the most unexpected places. Even as populations shrink, that need for connection never really fades. So, as the traveler moves on, he carries with him the stories of these towns—their struggles, their little victories, and the quiet strength that keeps them going. The heartland might not be thriving like it once did, but its spirit? That’s far from broken. If there’s one thing this journey teaches, it’s that resilience often looks like ordinary people simply doing their best, day after day.

Chapter 7: Encounters with Outsiders and the Edges of Belonging.
Not every stop along the road feels welcoming, does it? There are some towns where, the moment you arrive, you know you’re an outsider. You can feel it in the way people look at you—curious, maybe even a little wary. Picture walking into a small café, and suddenly, conversations drop to a hush. Folks glance up from their coffee, sizing you up.
It’s not outright hostility—more like a quiet caution, a kind of guardedness that tells you strangers don’t often pass through, and when they do, they're met with a healthy dose of skepticism.
In one of these places, the traveler meets a woman who understands this feeling all too well. She moved here from a distant city and remembers what it was like to be new. She shares her story—how tricky it was to fit in, to pick up on all those unspoken rules and little customs that shape everyday life. At first, she felt invisible. No matter how hard she tried to make friends, she’d get polite smiles and little else.
But over time, things changed. She started volunteering at the local school, joined the church choir, and made a point to show up for community events. “It takes patience,” she tells the traveler, “and a willingness to listen more than you talk.”
The traveler can’t help but reflect on how belonging isn’t something you’re handed. It’s built up slowly, moment by moment—through shared experiences and those small acts of kindness that add up over time.
In some towns, the sense of community is powerful, but it’s also a little closed off, shaped by generations of living side by side. Outsiders often feel like they’re intruding. But here’s the thing—outsiders can also bring new energy, fresh ideas, and a different perspective. The woman’s story is a gentle reminder that even the most tradition-bound places can change, but it takes both persistence and respect to earn your place.
And then there are moments that surprise you. In a town where the traveler feels the most out of place, a mechanic fixes a flat tire and refuses any payment. “Just pay it forward,” he says with a shrug. It’s a small gesture, but it sticks with the traveler—a quiet reminder that kindness can slip past even the thickest walls.
As the journey goes on, the traveler becomes more and more aware of the subtle ways communities draw their boundaries—who gets included, who’s left standing on the outside, and how those lines can shift, sometimes when you least expect it.
The search for the lost continent isn’t just about finding a place that feels like home. It’s really about understanding what it means to belong, and how that sense of belonging is created, tested, and renewed, one encounter at a time.

Chapter 8: The Shadows of the Past
Some towns wear their history like a badge. But others? They feel almost haunted by it.
Picture this: our traveler finds himself in a place where the past is just impossible to ignore. Old factories stand over the river, their windows broken, graffiti covering the crumbling walls. There’s a heaviness to the silence here, only broken now and then by a distant train rumbling through.
One afternoon, he meets a former mill worker—now in his seventies—who’s got stories to tell. He talks about those long shifts, the strong unions, and the solidarity that held folks together. There were strikes, sure, but there was music and laughter too. Nearly every family had someone working at the plant. “We thought it would last forever,” the old man says, and you can hear both pride and sorrow in his voice. Losing the mills didn’t just hurt people’s wallets. It left a real wound in the town’s identity.
Later, the traveler stops by the local museum. Faded photographs, yellowed newspaper clippings—they all tell the story of rise and decline. There’s nostalgia here, but also a quiet anger. Maybe you’ve felt it before—that frustration when big decisions are made far away, or markets shift, and suddenly everything changes. Here, the past isn’t just a memory. It’s alive. It shapes how people see themselves, and what they think the future might hold.
But even in a place like this, you can spot signs of renewal. A group of young artists has moved into those empty factory buildings, turning them into studios and galleries. They’re hosting open houses, running workshops, and inviting the whole community to check out what they’re creating. Some folks are skeptical. Others? They’re just curious—maybe even a little hopeful.
The traveler goes to one of these art shows and watches as old and new residents mingle, swapping stories and ideas. It’s a small thing, but it feels important—a spark of something new flickering in the shadows of the past.
So, what’s the takeaway? The shadows of the past can be long, but they don’t cover everything. The traveler leaves with a mix of sadness and hope, realizing that history can weigh us down, sure—but it can also give us strength and inspiration. This lost continent isn’t just a place for nostalgia. It’s a landscape where the past and present are always in conversation, shaping what comes next.

Chapter 9. The Road as a Mirror.
After weeks spent out there, moving mile after mile, the traveler starts to realize just how much the road has changed him.
You know those long hours behind the wheel—when the towns flicker by, and the scenery keeps shifting? It almost feels like a kind of meditation. The car becomes this safe little cocoon, but also a confessional. It’s the one place where your thoughts can really wander, and old memories suddenly float to the surface.
Of course, there are moments of loneliness too. Sometimes the road just stretches on, endlessly, and the only voice you hear is the one coming from the radio. But then, there are these moments of real clarity—when the world outside your windshield feels huge, but somehow close and familiar at the same time.
That’s when the traveler starts reflecting on his own life. He thinks about the choices he’s made, those roads he never took, and the people he’s left behind. The search for small-town America turns into something deeper—a search for meaning, for a sense of place in a world that can sometimes feel unanchored and rootless.
In one little town, he meets a man who’s never left. This guy runs the same hardware store his dad did, and every day, it’s the same routine. “Some people need to see the world,” the man tells him, “but I like knowing where I belong.”
The traveler can’t help but feel a bit envious of that certainty. At the same time, he wonders what it would be like to stay put, to really let your roots dig deep in one place.
The road shows him both the beauty—and the limits—of freedom. There’s this electric joy in always moving, in discovering something new around every bend. But there’s also that quiet ache for connection, for a place that feels like home.
Eventually, he realizes the journey isn’t just about finding some lost continent. It’s about understanding that tug-of-war inside us—the pull between wanting to roam and needing to belong, between longing and finding your place.
By the end of this stretch, the traveler feels both tired and grateful. The road has turned into a mirror, reflecting not just the country outside, but who he is on the inside.
And so, the search continues—shaped by every lesson, every mile, and every quiet moment along the way.

Chapter 10: The Enduring Spirit of Small-Town America
Picture this—our traveler, nearing the end of a long journey, finds himself in a small town buzzing with excitement. The annual festival is just about to begin. Banners are strung from every lamppost, and the whole place smells like barbecue. Laughter fills the air. Kids dart through the streets, faces painted with bright colors, while parents settle into folding chairs lining the parade route. For just one day, the town feels more alive than ever—almost as if the daily worries melt away, replaced by pure celebration.
The traveler can’t help but get swept up in it all. He grabs a slice of homemade pie, strikes up an easy conversation with a stranger, and lets himself feel the rush as fireworks crackle overhead. There’s a joy in these moments—something delicate, yet somehow lasting. It's a powerful reminder that real community isn’t just about shared history, but about coming together to make memories like this.
As the festival winds down, the traveler finds a quiet bench and settles in, watching those last sparks from the fireworks fade into the night sky. He starts to reflect. All those towns he visited, the people he met, the stories they shared—every place had its own flavor, its own hurdles. But there’s this thread running through it all: a deep belief in community, and a stubborn hope that keeps folks going, no matter the odds.
And you know, the so-called lost continent? It’s not really a place at all. It’s a patchwork of moments and memories, built by people who look out for each other and truly care about where they live. For the traveler, this journey has been something special—not just a search, but a kind of homecoming. It’s about finding peace with what’s come before, and opening up to what’s happening right now.
As he turns the car toward home, there’s this feeling of both completion and possibility. The road is still there, always waiting. There’ll be another trip, another story, another chance to find meaning in the simple things.

As we wrap up this journey through small-town America, I want you to take a moment to think about the places that shaped you. Maybe it’s a familiar street, a favorite diner, or just the way the light hits your childhood home. These stories remind us that even as the world changes, the heart of a small town endures—thanks to quiet acts of resilience and those simple, everyday gestures of kindness.
Belonging? Well, that doesn’t just happen overnight. It grows slowly—built on patience, on listening, and all those little moments shared with others. And sure, the past leaves its mark, but there’s always a chance for renewal. No matter how long the road gets, or how complicated the answers seem, there’s beauty—and maybe even a little bit of freedom—to be found along the way.
Community isn’t just a word. It’s felt in celebrations, in struggles, and in those simple connections that make you feel at home. So, as you look back on these stories, remember: the search for meaning never really ends. The places you hold dear might have changed, but the spirit you loved is still out there. Maybe it’s in a neighbor’s wave, a shared meal, or a festival that lights up the whole town for just one night.
Don’t be afraid to wander back down those old roads, to seek out the quiet corners where your memories and hopes meet. The lost continent? It’s not truly lost—it lives on, in every heart that cares enough to look for it, and in all the everyday moments that keep our communities alive.
Wherever your path leads next, carry these lessons with you. You’re part of a story that’s still unfolding—so keep searching, keep connecting, and remember: you play a part in keeping that spirit alive.
